pages.name: Two brackets, one x
pages.text: Both brackets hold the same `x`, so one pointer feeds both bars. If two numbers multiply to zero, at least one is zero: if the first is not zero, divide both sides by it, and the second is 0 ÷ the first, which is 0. So the product bar reaches zero only where the `x − 2` or the `x − 5` bar does, at `x = 2` and `x = 5`.

pages.name: Read the roots
pages.task: Values of `x` that make an equation true are its [[roots]], a different job from a square root. Which are the roots of `(x − 2)(x − 5) = 0`?
pages.why: A product is zero only when at least one of its factors is zero. `x − 2` is zero at `x = 2`, and `x − 5` at `x = 5`. Put each back and you get `0 × −3 = 0` and `3 × 0 = 0`.

pages.name: Opposite signs
pages.text: Each bracket is zero at the number that cancels it, so `x + 2` is zero at `x = −2`, and `x − 5` at `x = 5`. Each root has the opposite sign to its bracket's number. The dot rides the U-shaped parabola from Functions and their graphs, and meets the axis at the roots.

pages.name: Plus signs
pages.why: Each bracket is zero at the number that cancels it. `x + 2` is zero at `x = −2`, and `x + 5` at `x = −5`. Put each back and you get `0 × 3 = 0` and `−3 × 0 = 0`.

pages.name: Equal to 10
pages.text: Set equal to 10, the product is 10 at `x = 0` and `x = 7`, where neither bracket is 10. So `x − 2 = 10` gives a wrong `x = 12`, where the product is 70. Expand first: `x² − 7x + 10 = 10`, so `x² − 7x = 0`, which is `x(x − 7) = 0`.

pages.task: Spot the slip. A worked answer to `x² − 5x = 6` goes `x(x − 5) = 6`, then `x = 6` or `x − 5 = 6`, so `x = 6` or `x = 11`. Which step is wrong?
pages.why: Setting each bracket to 6 works only for a product of 0. Take the 6 across first: `x² − 5x − 6 = 0` factorises to `(x − 6)(x + 1) = 0`, so `x = 6` or `x = −1`. Both check, since `36 − 30 = 6` and `1 + 5 = 6`, but 11 makes 66.

pages.text: Dividing `x² = 6x` by `x` leaves `x = 6` alone, and loses `x = 0`. Take `6x` across instead, so `x(x − 6) = 0`, which gives `x = 0` or `x = 6`. Dividing by `x` is safe only when `x` cannot be 0.

pages.name: Dividing by x
pages.why: Take `4x` across rather than dividing by `x`. `x² − 4x = 0` is `x(x − 4) = 0`, so `x = 0` or `x = 4`. Dividing by `x` would have lost the 0.

pages.name: Plus or minus
pages.text: `x² = 9` has two roots, because a negative number times itself is positive too. Take the 9 across, so `x² − 9 = 0`, which is `(x + 3)(x − 3) = 0`. So `x = 3` or `x = −3`, written `x = ±3`.

pages.name: A number in front
pages.why: Divide both sides by 3, which is safe since 3 is never 0, so `x² = 16`. Then `x² − 16 = 0` is `(x + 4)(x − 4) = 0`, so `x = 4` or `x = −4`. Both check, since `3 × 16 = 48`.

pages.name: One root only
pages.text: `x² − 6x + 9` is `(x − 3)²`, so both bars are `x − 3` and reach zero together, at `x = 3` only. A square is never below zero, so the parabola touches the axis at 3 and turns back up.

pages.task: Solve `x² + x − 12 = 0`. The bars show its two brackets.
pages.why: `x + 4` is zero at `x = −4`, and `x − 3` at `x = 3`. Put each back and you get `16 − 4 − 12 = 0` and `9 + 3 − 12 = 0`. The brackets are the factorised form, not the answer.

pages.name: Mixed: zero first
pages.why: Take the −20 across first, so `x² + 9x + 20 = 0`. That is `(x + 4)(x + 5) = 0`, so `x = −4` or `x = −5`. Both check, since `−4 × 5 = −20` and `−5 × 4 = −20`.

pages.name: Mixed: the box
pages.task: In Calculus fundamentals, the volume of the box cut from a 30 cm sheet had slope `12x² − 240x + 900`. Solve `12x² − 240x + 900 = 0`.
pages.why: Every term divides by 12, which is never 0, so `x² − 20x + 75 = 0`, which is `(x − 5)(x − 15) = 0`. So `x = 5` or `x = 15`. Both check: `300 − 1,200 + 900 = 0` and `2,700 − 3,600 + 900 = 0`. At 15 cm the cuts meet and there is no box, so 5 cm is the cut that course found.
